argument: Byung-Chul Han argues that modern achievement societies control people not through prohibition ('negative power') but by telling everyone they can be anything they want ('positive power'), which makes each person the sole judge of their own worth with no outside reference point. Because that constant inward focus removes any other place for attention to go, it funnels people into narcissism, not as a personal failing but as one of the only lanes society leaves open, and it produces depression and anxiety through self-exploitation rather than external repression. Han's diagnosis is that what disappears in this world is genuine contact with 'the other,' and his prescription is to deliberately reintroduce listening, contemplation, and activities pursued purely for joy rather than self-optimization.
keyIdeas: Han distinguishes negative power, which controls through prohibition ('you should not'), from positive power, which controls through open-ended possibility ('you can'); positive power is more effective because people end up policing themselves.

Making someone the sole arbiter of their own standards, both setting the bar and checking whether they meet it, removes any outside reference point and turns attention permanently inward, which Han says produces narcissism.

Han reverses the common explanation for rising narcissism: individuals aren't causing a narcissistic world through bad parenting; rather, the ethos of achievement society funnels people into narcissism because it's one of the only lanes available.
The same neoliberal logic that deregulates businesses gets applied to the self: with no outside authority regulating you, you become responsible for constantly increasing your own market value.

Han calls the resulting psychological state depression rather than repression, because there's no external force holding people down; instead people 'auto-exploit,' becoming both master and slave to themselves, and Han's remedy is to make space for truly listening to others and for activities pursued purely for joy.

terms.def: Han's term for a society controlled through positive power ('you can be anything') rather than the disciplinary prohibitions of earlier eras.
Negative power controls by saying 'should' (prohibition); positive power controls by saying 'can' (open-ended possibility), which Han argues is more effective.

Han's term, used directly in the episode ('we're encouraged to auto-exploit ourselves'), for people voluntarily exploiting their own labor and mind as both master and slave, with no external oppressor to blame or resist.
Han's term for genuine difference or otherness in another person or idea, which narcissistic self-focus increasingly forecloses.
An economic and political strategy of deregulating businesses to spur growth, which Han argues gets applied to individuals as pressure to constantly self-optimize.
